title: Place n queens on an n-by-n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other, and return all distinct solutions (or the count).
shortTitle: N-Queens: place queens row by row, check conflicts
keyPoints: Place one queen per row; for each row try every column and backtrack when a row has no safe column
Track conflicts with three sets: used columns, row-minus-column diagonals, and row-plus-column diagonals
A cell is safe when its column, row-col, and row+col are all absent from the three sets, giving O(1) checks
Placing a queen adds three keys; backtracking removes them, maintaining the constraint sets
When the row index reaches n, all queens are placed without conflict and one solution is recorded
The pruning keeps the real search far below the naive n^n bound, though it remains super-polynomial
Optimizations include first-row symmetry halving and bitmask-based constraint tracking

s1_definition.oneliner: One queen per row; a column is safe if its column and both diagonals are free; backtrack when a row is stuck.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **N-Queens** – place n chess queens on an n-by-n board so that no two share a row, column, or diagonal.
- **Row-by-row backtracking** – fill one row at a time, trying each column and placing a queen only where no conflict exists.
- **Constraint sets** – three sets track occupied columns, occupied `row - col` diagonals, and occupied `row + col` diagonals for O(1) conflict checks.
- **Backtracking** – place a queen (add three keys), recurse to the next row, then remove the three keys to try the next column.
- **Complexity** – far below n^n due to pruning, but still super-polynomial.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must place n audit checkpoints on an n-by-n scheduling grid where no two checkpoints may share a column or a diagonal time slot. A scheduler fills one row at a time, placing a checkpoint only in a safe column, and backs up whenever a row has no safe spot.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  N-Queens Backtracking (n=4)

  Row 0: try col 0,1,2,3
  Row 1: try cols not in {col, diag1, diag2}
  Row 2: same constraint check
  Row 3: same constraint check -> if all placed, record

  Constraint sets for O(1) check:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ cols:  which columns are taken         │
  │ diag1: which (row - col) are taken     │
  │ diag2: which (row + col) are taken     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Solution 1:        Solution 2:
  . Q . .            . . Q .
  . . . Q            Q . . .
  Q . . .            . . . Q
  . . Q .            . Q . .
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
N-Queens is the classic constraint-satisfaction backtracking problem. You place one queen per row and for each row try every column, placing a queen only where it does not conflict with any already-placed queen. The key to fast conflict detection is tracking three sets: occupied columns, one diagonal family keyed by row - col, and the other keyed by row + col. A cell is safe when all three lookups miss.

Placing a queen adds three keys to the sets, recursing fills the next row, and backtracking removes the keys. Reaching row n means all queens are safely placed and you record the configuration. The pruning from the three sets keeps the real search far below the naive n^n bound.

The bitmask optimization replaces the three sets with three integers and uses bitwise operations to find free columns in just a few instructions, which is much faster for large n. Symmetry-based pruning can nearly halve the work by only exploring the first half of columns in the first row.

At the National Bank of India, compliance used this pattern to assign n audit checkpoints to a scheduling grid where no two could share a column or diagonal, finding all valid arrangements efficiently with constant-time conflict checks.

Remember one sentence: one queen per row, three constraint sets for O(1) diagonal checks, and backtrack when a row has no safe column.
